title: The Pumpkin That Ate a Bicycle

pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 29: Growing: pea (19 cm). Also: a pumpkin. (See below.)*

Theo did not wait for the soil to settle. He had a seed in his hand, a small, wrinkled orange pumpkin, and he shoved it into a hole in the dirt with the speed of someone trying to hide a crime. He patted the earth flat, stepped back, and looked at me with eyes that were bright and very uncertain.

"I'm... good at plants?" he said.

It was the true thing. It had to be.

"It has to be true," I said. "Actually true."

Theo shrugged. He looked at the dirt, then at Gherkin, who was watching from under the pear tree with the intensity of a teacher checking for missing pencils.

"Mm," Gherkin said.

I counted. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"Is it," the tortoise finished, taking his time as if he were chewing a particularly tough leaf.

Theo’s face went the color of the pumpkin. He looked like he wanted to un-say it, which, I was learning, was impossible.
pages.image: A boy in a beanie and hoodie stands awkwardly in a garden, looking at a tiny hole in the dirt; a mossy tortoise watches from under a pear tree; the boy looks uncertain and slightly panicked.

pages.text:
We went home. I told myself the garden would be sensible. I told myself the rule was one true thing, and we had given it one. I did not check the seed. I did not check the sky. I slept for four hours and woke up with the sound of tearing fabric.

I ran out the back door. Theo was already there, standing in the path, his hands in his pockets, looking at the green wall that used to be a path.

The pumpkin vine had erupted. It was a green fountain, a thick, muscular rope of leaves and tendrils that had swallowed the wheelbarrow, half the gravel path, and the rusted tin. It had also swallowed Theo’s skateboard, which he had left leaning against the wall.

At the center of the mess sat the pumpkin. It was the size of a small car. It was perfectly round, deep orange, and it was, unmistakably, sulking.
pages.image: A massive orange pumpkin sits in a garden path, surrounded by thick green vines that have swallowed a wheelbarrow and a skateboard; a boy in a beanie stands in the background looking shocked.

pages.text:
"We cut it," Theo said, pulling a pocket knife from his hoodie. He saw me shaking my head and put it away, though the blade had already made a small, sharp promise in the air.

"Rule four," I said, my voice flat. "Never hurry a root."

"We pull it," he suggested, as if this were a reasonable alternative to waiting for the sun to move. He grabbed a thick tendril and yanked with both hands. The vine snapped back like a rubber band, slapping him squarely in the face. He rubbed his cheek, wincing, while the green wall rustled with what I chose to interpret as amusement.

A small head popped up from behind the pumpkin. Yusuf. He had no idea how he had gotten there, which is to say he had likely climbed, jumped, or simply appeared, because he was six and the rules of physics seemed to be suggestions to him. He looked at the giant orange sphere, then at us, then back at the pumpkin with the serious concentration he usually reserved for finding lost socks.

He lay down on the grass, pressed his ear against the cool skin of the pumpkin, and whispered, "Sorry."

It did nothing. The vine did not shrink. The pumpkin did not apologize. But it was the sweetest thing anyone had said to anything all week, and the air around us felt slightly less tangled, or maybe I was just tired.

"Mm," Gherkin said from the shadows, his voice slow and thick like molasses. "Not... that."
pages.image: A small boy with missing front teeth lies on the grass, ear pressed against a giant orange pumpkin; a boy in a beanie stands nearby, rubbing his cheek; a tortoise watches from under a tree.

pages.text:
Theo stared at the pumpkin. His face was red, not from anger, but from the effort of holding something back. He looked at his knee, then at the sky, then at me.

"I'm not good at plants," he said. His voice was very small. "My grandmother died in March. I never learned. I've been sitting on staircases for three months because it's the only place nobody asks me about it."

The air in the garden went still. The wind stopped. Even the birds seemed to hold their breath.

The green muscle of the vine began to retract. It pulled itself back, inch by inch, like a tide going out. The wheelbarrow dropped with a clang. The skateboard slid free and landed gently on the grass, as neatly as a waiter setting down a plate.

The pumpkin shrank. It stopped at the size of a cabbage. It sat there, solid and real, no longer a monster, just a vegetable.
pages.image: A boy in a beanie stands with his head down, looking at a normal-sized pumpkin on the grass; a skateboard lies neatly beside it; the garden is quiet and still; a tortoise watches from under a tree.

pages.text:
Nobody spoke. It was a good silence, the kind that settles over a room after the thunder stops. I watched Theo scuff his shoe against the dirt, tracing lines in the gravel like he was drawing a map of somewhere he wanted to be.

"I'm sorry about your grandmother," I said.

The words came out before I could stop them. They felt different in my chest than usual, solid and true, like they had been waiting for me to find them.

Theo looked up. He glanced at the pumpkin, then back at the ground. He didn't say thank you. He didn't say it was okay. He just gave a small, sharp nod.

Behind us, the bench began to hum. It was a low, warm vibration that traveled through the wood and into the air, exactly the way a fridge works when the door is closed tight. It felt like the bench had been waiting a very long time for someone to say the right thing.
pages.image: A boy and a girl stand in a garden, looking at each other; a small pumpkin sits on the grass nearby; a wooden bench hums in the background; the scene is quiet and intimate.
